And a great city in outer India fell,
and one hundred and fifty thousand people were brought out from under the dust of the courtyards that were overturned,
and they were buried.
And in the year 1207
[1207] of the Greeks (896 of our Lord?), Leo, emperor of the Romans, fell ill with abdominal pain and died;
and his son Alexander reigned after him for one year.
And because he turned his heart away from the fear of God,
and gave himself over to sorcerers and enchanters,
he was struck down with the rod of justice and died.
And after him reigned his brother Constantine for four years.
And at the beginning of his reign, Simeon, the chief of the Bulgars and Slavs, came against Constantinople,
and he devastated many villages.
And he also besieged the city,
and made a great trench against it from Blachernae to the gate called the Golden [Gate].
Then the emperor of the Romans sent to him, [saying]:
"Since we are all Christians, children of one baptism,
why are there such contentions between us?" But when he could not be persuaded to be reconciled,
then the emperor Constantine gathered the Arab prisoners who were in Constantinople,
and he promised them
that if they helped the Romans toward victory over the Bulgars,
he would set them free.
And when they swore to the emperor,
weapons were given to them.
And the Romans went out together with the Arabs in full accord,
and they defeated the Slavs.
And they killed many of them,
and the rest fled.
The emperor, however, went back on his promise,
and took the weapons from them,
and cast them into irons again,
and scattered them throughout his territories,
for he feared lest they should raise their heads [in revolt].
For this narrative is related by the blessed Mar Michael [as occurring] in a war between the Romans and the Arabs,
whereas the Arabic records report it [as occurring] in the war with the Slavs;
and this [latter] is the correct one.
For in a war against the Arabs,
the Romans would not have trusted [enough] to loose Arab prisoners from their chains
and to put weapons into their hands.
And in this same year,
the Arabs of Baghdad gathered against a certain young servant of Abu Ghalib, a Christian physician of the caliph,
and they testified against him that he had reviled their prophet,
and they wished to kill him.
However, the caliph al-Mu'tadid, when he heard [it], said
that the Arabs were falsely accusing [him].
